newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: EVANS SAYS RBA TOO CONSERVATIVE ON INTERST RATES
The Shadow Treasurer, Gareth Evans, says the Reserve Bank has a huge responsibility to move the economy along because the federal Government has abandoned any commitment to job growth.
Mr Evans says another interest rate cut is needed to boost growth and employment.
Mr Evans says he's disappointed that Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane is being so conservative with interest rate changes.
Mr Macfarlane last night indicated the Reserve Bank is unlikely to change interest rates until it knows the outcome of the ACTU's living wage case.
TOUGHER LAWS FOR TRANSPORT INDUSTRY
National laws are being proposed to prosecute transport operators, freight forwarders and even customers for truck driving offences.
The National Road Transport Commission says all States and Territories support the draft legislation which could result in corporations being fined thousands of dollars.
The proposal is similar to Workcare and other legislation which already provides for prosecution of companies and others with any part in the decision to break the law.
The new legislation could be operating as early as the middle of next year.
LEGAL ACTION OVER CARMEN LAWRENCE'S LEGAL FEES
Legal action has started against the Federal Government to try to recover legal fees incurred by former Federal Health Minister, Carmen Lawrence, in the 1995 Marks Royal Commission.
Law firm Dunhill Madden Butler has issued proceedings in the Federal Court in Sydney to recover more than half a million dollars.
The Marks Royal Commission found Dr Lawrence was untruthful about her knowledge of a petition tabled in State parliament.
The Managing Partner of Dunhill Madden Butler, John Churchill, says the firm is relying on advice from former Liberal Attorney-General Bob Ellicott QC.
KERNOT ATTACKS PM OVER PAY RISE
The Australian Democrats leader wants to know why the Prime Minister approved a pay rise for a member of Senator Mal Colston's staff just before the independent voted for the part sale of Telstra.
Senator Kernot says she doesn't accept it's a co-incidence that the Prime Minister approved the rise, on the eve of the Senate vote on the Telstra legislation.
She says there's a question mark over what motivated the prime minister to approve the pay rise when he was preaching to everyone else about budgetary constraints.
The Opposition claims the increase will cost up to 75-thousand dollars.
LITERACY RESULTS PRIVATE: MINISTER
New South Wales Education minister John Aquilina has given a guarantee that literacy test results won't be made public.

Yesterday, the State Government announced an 18-point-four million dollar package, which includes a test of students' reading abilities at the start of high school, on top of basic skills tests in Years Three and Five.
But the Teachers Federation threatened to ban the tests, saying if the results were made public it would threaten students' privacy.
A spokesman for Mr Aquilina says although the results will be available to schools and parents, it's against the law for anyone to publish the results.
NATIONAL BACKBENCHER WANTS CONVENTION VOTING CHANGED
National Party backbencher, Ian Sinclair, says it's not fair for the two territories to have only one elected delegate each at the People's Convention on the Constitution.
Mr Sinclair wants the Government's proposed system for chosing the convention delegates changed to allow for a group rather than individuals to attend.
He says the Northern Territory and ACT should at least have the chance to send a republican and a monarchist to the convention.
The Government's proposed scheme will see voters in New South Wales and Victoria choose half the 76 elected convention delegates.
Queensland would have 13 elected delegates, Western Australia nine, South Australia eight, Tasmania six, and the two Territories one each.
